Who handles your Albany tax bill

Albany splits the work between two city offices. The Treasurer takes in payments and the Assessor decides the value behind the bill. You will find the Treasurer at 24 Eagle Street in City Hall, 518-434-5036. The Assessor works upstairs in Room 302, reachable at 518-434-5155. The City Charter names the Treasurer chief fiscal officer, responsible for collecting every city tax and any other money the city is owed.

  • Treasurer: bills, payments, receipts, changes of address, returned payments
  • Assessor: values, STAR and other exemption forms, grievance forms, parcel maps
  • Board of Assessment Review: hears complaints about assessments, with members appointed by the Common Council to five-year terms

Due dates and late charges

Pay the whole bill, or the first half, by January 31. Seniors who qualify get until February 6. If a deadline lands on a weekend it slides to the next business day, and since January 31 falls on a Sunday in 2027, the working deadline that year is Monday, February 1.

All owners may now pay in halves. The first half is due at the deadline. The second is billed in early July and may be paid any time after the first, plus interest. The online system accepts full payments only, so a split payment has to go by check or cash.

Bills are meant to arrive by January 12. Missing yours? Print a copy from the Treasurer's online lookup. Penalties for late payment are mandatory under state law, and the city has no power to waive the interest. A returned payment costs $34.

The waste collection fee

This $180 per unit charge sits on the tax bill itself. Until 2026 it came as its own mailing. When a prior year's fee goes unpaid (it was $90 per unit for 2025), the balance moves onto the next tax bill with late charges added. If you think the fee should not apply to your property, email the Treasurer or call 518-434-5036 and ask for an exemption application. Owners the city already knew were exempt in 2023 and 2024 were not billed in 2025.

For a seller the point is simple: an old unpaid fee is part of what you owe at closing. Ask the Treasurer for a payoff that includes it, then check that total against the January bill in your hands.

Ways to pay

Mail, the website and City Hall all work. Skip bill-payment services if you can. Their envelopes tend to carry no postmark, and Albany counts the USPS postmark only, never a postage meter stamp.

MailCheck payable to City of Albany, sent to City Treasurer, Room 109, City Hall, Albany, NY 12207. Include the bill number, your signature, the date and any interest owed.

A self-addressed stamped envelope gets you a receipt immediately. Without one, receipts are mailed in bulk in late March or April. Online receipts post within 48 hours.

Appealing your assessment

The window opens May 1 and closes on Grievance Day, the fourth Tuesday in May. Pick up the form at the Assessor's office once May 1 arrives and return it by that Tuesday. Complaints go before the Board of Assessment Review under Chapter 42 of the Albany General Code.

Assessments move when buildings are built, burned or torn down, and when the city refreshes the whole roll to keep it even. Parcel maps are available to view at the Assessor's office. The board weighs market value and ignores how heavy the bill feels, so show it a recent sale of a comparable house nearby, a repair estimate or an appraisal.

Exemptions and STAR

Apply for exemptions at the Assessor's office between January 1 and March 1. Basic STAR is meant for owners who live in the house. All owners sign the form and attach a photocopy of a driver's license showing residence. For Enhanced STAR help, call 518-434-5155.

New York's Tax Department pays STAR as a credit. You register once, the payment arrives ahead of school tax, and it continues yearly as long as you stay eligible. On a sale, end your registration. The buyer signs up after the house becomes a primary residence.

Selling with taxes owed

At closing, any open balance comes out of your proceeds and the current year is divided between you and the buyer on the closing statement. No check is needed at the table, but the figure has to be exact, so get it from the Treasurer, at 518-434-5036 on weekdays, before the closing date.

  • Request the current balance, including any waste fee carried over, and save the reply by email
  • If the first half is paid and the July half has not been billed yet, the buyer typically gets a credit for the months you owned
  • Confirm with the Assessor that your exemption ends or moves in line with the new owner's status

A cash buyer can take over the same payoff and still close fast. Owing the city does not end a sale; it changes only what is left for you once the statement is settled. Gather the parcel number, your last bill and your mailing address before calling so the answer comes back the same day.

Before you list

Sellers get better results when the paperwork is lined up before a buyer appears. Start with the tax side, because it is the part that cannot be guessed.

  1. Print your current bill from the online lookup and note whether it is paid in full or by installment.
  2. Check the bill for the waste collection fee, including any amount left over from last year.
  3. Ask the Assessor whether any exemption is on the parcel and how it should be handled at transfer.
  4. Write down who will answer questions for you at the closing, and give that person the Treasurer's number.

These steps take little time and head off the usual delay, a payoff figure that arrives late or differs from the closing statement.

The Albany seller

Albany has about 101,698 residents, and owners occupy about 38.2 percent of homes. The median value of an owner-occupied home is $234,700. Much of the older housing near the river is row houses, with roofs, porches and boilers a buyer will want inspected. With so many rentals, plenty of sellers own small multifamily buildings and should confirm each unit's waste fee before requesting a payoff.

Frequently asked questions

What is the Albany property tax deadline?

January 31, or February 6 for eligible seniors. A weekend deadline moves to the next business day, which makes it February 1 in 2027. Mailed payments are judged by USPS postmark.

Can I split my Albany tax bill into two payments?

Yes. Half is due at the January deadline and the rest after the July bill, with interest added. Only checks or cash work for installments, not the online system.

Where do I get a copy of my Albany tax bill or receipt?

Use the Treasurer's online lookup or email the Treasurer's billing address. Mailed receipts go out in bulk in late March or April, and online receipts show up within 48 hours.

When is Albany Grievance Day?

The fourth Tuesday in May. Forms are at the Assessor's office, City Hall Room 302, from May 1, and the complaint has to be filed by that day.

Do I owe Albany tax if I sell mid-year?

Only for the months you owned. The closing statement divides the year, and any unpaid balance goes to the Treasurer out of your proceeds, so ask for the payoff before closing.

Which Amherst office answers what

A bill here has several layers, so know who answers which question. The Town Clerk's office also serves as Receiver of Taxes and collects the Town and County bill. The Assessor's Office sets assessed values. Both are in Town Hall at 5583 Main Street in Williamsville. Amherst is a suburb of Buffalo in northern Erie County, and the town includes the village of Williamsville plus hamlets such as Eggertsville, Getzville, Snyder, Swormville and East Amherst.

Town and County due date

February 15 is the date. If it falls on a weekend, Town Hall pushes the deadline out to the next day it is open. The Clerk's counter keeps taking full and partial payments through June 30, but penalties start accruing once the deadline passes.

Counter hours are 8:30 a.m. to 4 p.m., Monday through Friday, with no lunch closing. The Town Hall back door has a drop box you can use at any hour; a payment placed there before midnight on the due date is on time.

Paying in one lump is optional. Send what you can, as often as needed, in any dollar amount. Just remember that the unpaid remainder is charged interest and penalties after the due date, following the schedule on the back of the bill.

Making sure a payment is not late

A mailbox drop is risky. Postmarks now show the day an envelope reaches a regional sorting hub, which may be one to three days after you mail it. Safer routes:

  • Have a clerk hand-stamp the envelope at a post office counter
  • Use certified or registered mail
  • Put it in the back-entrance drop box at Town Hall
  • Pay online through the town website, searching your owner name or address in the tax bill lookup
  • Walk it in to the Town Clerk's window

Avoid your bank's bill pay. Those checks come in bulk mail from a processing center and carry no postmark, and the town says users of that route take the risk themselves.

How to challenge your assessment

Start by asking the Assessor's Office for an informal review. If that does not settle it, file a formal complaint on form RP-524 before Grievance Day. The next Grievance Day is Tuesday, May 25, 2027, and hearing details are posted after May 1. Informal review information goes up each year after March 1. Separate review applications exist for residential, condominium, commercial and vacant land parcels.

Levies are not the Assessor's call, so argue market value. Your best evidence is sales of like houses nearby, matched for location, style, age and size; a five-year-old house and a fifty-year-old house are poor matches. The Board of Assessment Review keeps what you hand in, so retain your own copies.

Buying or selling in the middle of the year

The person who owns the parcel on the due date is liable for the whole bill, even when no bill showed up. A buyer who closes mid-year still owes the entire bill, though the closing statement normally prorates it and the seller credits the buyer for the months before the purchase. The attorney handling the closing calculates that credit, and the seller does not send a partial payment to the tax collector.

Selling? The closing attorney should pay any unpaid current tax out of your proceeds, so compare the closing statement figure with the Receiver's own number. If the name or mailing address on the bill is wrong, the Assessor corrects it, not the Town Clerk. Fix that before listing so the bill does not go astray during the sale.

The Assessor also fields questions about the RPTL charge on a Town and County bill. That line can reflect one-time charges rather than regular tax, so ask before you assume a payoff is wrong.

Housing in the town

About 130,442 people lived in Amherst as of July 2025. Roughly 69.9 percent of homes are owner-occupied, with a median home value of $311,600 and median gross rent of $1,393. Figures cover the whole town, including Williamsville and the hamlets, so a given street can run above or below them.

What a seller should gather

Collect a few records before you talk to a buyer, so every number you quote is current. You will want the latest Town and County bill, any receipt for partial payments, and the school tax bill from your district. If the house is in Williamsville, add the village bill. Note the owner name and mailing address as they appear on the bill, because a mismatch with the deed is the sort of small error that holds up a closing.

Next, decide how you want to handle the closing. A cash buyer will usually use a title company or an attorney, who orders the payoff figures, prorates the current year and pays each tax office from your proceeds. Your job is to give that person accurate contact details and to read the statement before signing. If a number looks off, call the relevant office the same day rather than waiting for the closing table. Keep the replies in writing so the title company can see exactly what each office told you and when.

Selling with tax due

Ask for the exact balance before closing, because partial payments, penalties and village charges can all change it. A short checklist keeps the sale on schedule:

  1. Call the Town Clerk at 716-631-7021 for the Town and County balance.
  2. If the property is in Williamsville, call the village clerk for the village portion.
  3. Ask your school district for its balance, since it bills on its own schedule.
  4. Confirm the owner name and mailing address on file with the Assessor.

A buyer paying cash can close on a short timeline. The payoffs come out of the sale price just as they would in a financed sale, so open tax rarely slows a closing once the figures are collected. If a buyer asks why the totals differ from your last bill, remember that penalties, partial payments and village charges move the balance. Send each office's figure to the closing attorney in writing, and compare them with the statement before you sign.

Frequently asked questions

What is the Amherst property tax due date?

Mid-February: the 15th. A weekend date gets pushed out by the town. The Clerk's office will take partial payments until June 30.

Can I pay Amherst taxes in installments?

In effect, yes. Any amount can be paid, as often as you like, though whatever remains after the due date builds interest and penalties on the schedule printed on the back of the bill.

Is there a drop box for Amherst tax payments?

Yes, at the back door of Town Hall, 5583 Main Street, available at all hours. A payment dropped there up to midnight on the due date counts as on time.

When is Amherst Grievance Day?

The next one is Tuesday, May 25, 2027. Formal complaints go on form RP-524, informal review details appear after March 1, and the Assessor at 716-631-7038 can walk you through either.

Who do I call about Williamsville village tax?

The Village of Williamsville Clerk's Office at 632-4120, option 9. The town's tax lookup shows Town, County and school tax for village properties, but not the village tax itself.

Where to pay and who sets the bill

Payments go to the Town of Brookhaven Receiver of Taxes during the collection season, December 1 to May 31, and then to the Suffolk County Comptroller. Visit Town Hall at 1 Independence Hill, Farmingville, or call 631-451-9009; the Assessor shares the building. The town runs from Port Jefferson and Stony Brook down to Patchogue and had 485,773 residents in 2020, so school districts and home prices differ widely under a single tax office.

Rates are not the Receiver's decision. Your school district writes the school budget, the county budget drives the county levy, and the Supervisor and Town Board set the town levy.

Tax year and when bills arrive

Suffolk County's tax year starts December 1 and ends November 30 of the next year. The lien attaches on the first day, and the town mails bills in mid-December, aiming for delivery by December 15. Nothing in your mailbox by the third week of December? Phone the tax office.

Each June 1 the online system closes for the year just ended, then reopens in December. Escrowed owners receive an informational copy around mid-July, because the lender is sent the bill to pay.

Due dates and late charges

Half the bill is due January 10, the other half May 31, and one bill may be paid in two parts. Interest on the first half climbs monthly after January 10. Anything unpaid after May 31 is delinquent.

Payment madeInterest added on the first half

Enhanced STAR recipients and owners with the over-65 exemption get five additional business days after May 31. After that, the Suffolk County Comptroller handles the account, charging a 5 percent penalty and 1 percent monthly interest running from February 1. The town stays out of delinquent accounts.

How to pay

Options are online, in person and mail, and postmarks decide a lot. Since a federal change on December 24, 2025, a letter dropped in a mailbox may not be stamped that day. Only a hand-stamped envelope from a post office counter is guaranteed by the town, and penalties cannot be waived when the postmark is late.

  • Online: e-check for $1.75, or a credit card with a 2.35 percent fee. Partial payments are not allowed online.
  • Drop box: outside the Town Hall front lobby, always open, no cash. A receipt follows by mail the next business day.
  • Walk-in: weekdays, 9 a.m. to 4 p.m.
  • Mail: send the right stub with the check, postmarked by January 10 for the first half and May 31 for the second half.

Either office accepts a partial payment of at least $200 plus interest due. A bounced check adds $20.

How to grieve an assessment

Grievances are taken from May 1 until Grievance Day, the third Tuesday of May, which in 2027 is May 18. The online form is open for that same stretch. Exemption applications are due by the March 1 taxable status date. The tentative roll appears May 1 and the final roll July 1.

A paper grievance goes to the Town of Brookhaven Assessor, Attention: Grievance, at 1 Independence Hill, or into the Assessor's bin at the main lobby security desk. Hearings are held at Town Hall on Grievance Day, so check the Grievance Day page each spring for the schedule.

There is no grace period: anything sent before May 1 or after Grievance Day comes back to you unprocessed.

Selling with taxes unpaid

Under Suffolk County law the owner must pay on time whether or not a bill came, and late payment brings penalties and interest. Because bills mail in December, anyone buying in the county later that year is told to phone the Receiver and verify that every tax is current.

  • Get a current figure from the Receiver, noting if only the first half or the full year is paid
  • Bill sent to an old address? Give the Receiver your correct mailing address
  • After May 31, ask the Suffolk County Comptroller for the payoff. The check address is 330 Center Drive in Riverhead.

Taxes still unpaid at the tax lien sale, which usually happens in December, lead the Comptroller to sell a lien to Suffolk County. A cash buyer can pay off a delinquent balance at closing the same way a lender would, which avoids that sale.

Exemptions and your bill

Exemption applications are tied to the March 1 taxable status date, so anything you want on the coming bill needs to be filed by then. Enhanced STAR and the over-65 exemption also carry the extra five business days after May 31 mentioned above. When you sell, tell the new owner which exemptions were in place. They may have to apply on their own, and a buyer who learns that late can end up with a larger bill than expected.

Ask the Assessor, who works from the same Town Hall building as the Receiver, how each exemption is handled when the deed changes hands. Write down the answer and pass it to your closing attorney.

When the bill and the sale overlap

Many Brookhaven closings fall between December and May, when one half of the bill may be paid and the other still open. Work out in advance which half you are covering. The same calendar matters if you close after May 31, because the Comptroller, not the town, then holds the account and quotes the payoff. Collecting that figure before the contract is signed prevents a late surprise.

Owners and housing in Brookhaven

Most Brookhaven homes (80.9 percent) are lived in by their owners. A July 2025 estimate put the population at 496,410, and the median owner-occupied home is worth $489,200, against median gross rent of $2,314. If your assessment seems out of step with comparable houses on your street, contact the Assessor before May.

Closing steps for a cash sale

In a cash deal, title work and payoffs set the pace. Follow this sequence:

  1. Get the current balance from the Receiver, or from the Comptroller after May 31.
  2. Confirm your mailing address is right so no bill goes astray.
  3. Give the figures to your closing attorney or title agent.
  4. Review the closing statement and make sure the tax line matches the number you were given.

Payoffs are deducted from your proceeds, so nothing comes out of pocket. Tell the closing attorney exactly which portions of the year are paid, so the buyer's credit is figured correctly. If a lien sale or delinquency is already on the record, mention it up front, since the payoff is higher after penalties and interest.

Frequently asked questions

When are Brookhaven property taxes due?

Two deadlines: January 10 for the first half, May 31 for the second. Miss the first and you pay another 1 percent per month, reaching 5 percent for payments in the final three weeks of May.

Who do I pay after May 31 in Brookhaven?

The Suffolk County Comptroller, on Center Drive in Riverhead. Expect a 5 percent penalty and 1 percent per month counted from February 1 to be added.

Can I pay Brookhaven tax by credit card?

Online, yes: the card carries a 2.35 percent bank fee, and an e-check is $1.75. The town keeps neither fee, and online payment cannot be partial.

When is Brookhaven Grievance Day?

Third Tuesday of May, meaning May 18 in 2027. Filing runs from May 1 to that day.

What if I never got a Brookhaven tax bill?

Yes, you owe the tax plus any penalties. If nothing has come by the third week of December, ring the Receiver of Taxes at 631-451-9009 and update your mailing address.

Due dates for the city and county bills

The city bill and the county bill come from different offices on different schedules. Ask the City of Buffalo Department of Assessment and Taxation for the current due dates on the city bill, and Erie County Real Property Tax Services for the county bill.

The city's Tax Office also prepares the delinquent tax notices required under section 593 of the City Charter. If you fall behind, the department helps owners obtain court-ordered payment plans, and it notifies owners facing foreclosure for non-payment. Call 716-851-5733 early rather than after a notice arrives.

Annual reassessment and how to appeal

Buffalo has returned to annual reassessments, and owners appeal during an annual grievance window. Ask the Department of Assessment and Taxation for this year's dates, and prepare your evidence before the window opens.

You file state form RP-524 with the department, and a board of city residents with real estate experience reviews it. The city's budget describes plans for electronic filing and self-scheduled hearings. The Assessor reviews every sale and every deed filed in the city, and inspects old and new buildings, demolitions and fire-damaged structures, which is why a recent sale next door can move your number.

The department also works with the Corporation Counsel on court cases that challenge a value and on small claims assessment review applications, so an owner who loses before the board still has a next step. Bring your own evidence to the first review: a closing statement, an appraisal, or photos of damage a field inspector could have missed.

Exemptions and STAR

The department processes applications and renewals for several programs under the state's property tax law:

  • School Tax Relief (STAR)
  • Senior citizen exemption for low-income owners
  • Exemption for persons with disabilities and limited income
  • Senior citizen longtime resident exemption
  • Alternative exemption for military service
  • Capital improvements exemption

The state Tax Department now pays STAR as a credit after you register once, and it issues the payment before school tax is due. If you sell, close that registration. A buyer registers once the house becomes their primary residence. Eligibility rules differ by program, so the Assessor's office is the place to confirm which ones your house qualifies for.

What a Buffalo tax foreclosure looks like

The city runs an In Rem foreclosure each year and ends it with an annual auction administered by the Tax Office. Owners who fall behind get notice first, and the department can help arrange a court-ordered payment plan. Erie County also conducts auctions and foreclosure proceedings for unpaid county tax through its Real Property Tax Services office.

For a payoff figure and payment options on any county account in that position, call 716-858-8333. Settling the balance before a sale closes keeps a lien from blocking the deed transfer.

Selling with taxes owed

City tax, sewer rent, the county bill and any local charges are paid from your sale proceeds at closing. Order payoff figures from both the city and Erie County, since they keep separate books.

  • Ask the city for tax, sewer rent and user fee balances, plus any sidewalk or demolition charge
  • Ask Erie County for the county balance, especially after January when the new county bill posts
  • If a parcel was combined or divided, the city accepts that application only after a full year of city tax, sewer rent and user fee is paid

A cash buyer can close quickly, and the payoffs are deducted the same way as in any other sale. Collect both figures in writing and hand them to the closing attorney so nothing is missed.

Sewer rent and local charges

Sewer rent arrives with the city's tax billing, and it is easy to overlook because it is not property tax. The department also bills local charges such as sidewalk or demolition costs, and these can stay on a parcel until they are paid. Treat them as part of the payoff. If you are unsure whether anything is attached to your address, ask the city for a full list of balances rather than a tax-only figure.

One more rule affects owners who plan to combine or split a lot before selling. The city takes that application only after a full year of city tax, sewer rent and user fee has been paid, so a parcel with arrears cannot be reconfigured until it is current.

What changes between the city bill and the county bill

It helps to think of two separate ledgers. The city keeps one for tax, sewer rent and user fees, and Erie County keeps another for the county bill. A balance on one does not show up on the other, which is why a seller who clears the city account can still be surprised by a county figure that posts later. After January, when the new county bill posts, ask the county for an updated number.

Each ledger has its own phone line, hours and payment options. Keep the two numbers, 716-851-5733 for the city and 716-858-8333 for the county, together in one place and note the date of every call. A buyer's title company will want the same information, and having it ready lets escrow open without delay.

Buffalo housing in brief

Fewer than half of Buffalo households own their home, with an owner-occupied rate of 43.0 percent. The median value of an owner-occupied home is $164,200 and median gross rent is $1,046. Neighborhoods such as Elmwood, Allentown, Larkinville and the First Ward each price differently. A lower assessment in the December window feeds into both the city and county bills, so it is worth checking before you list.

Preparing for a quick Buffalo sale

Buffalo sellers often have more than one bill to clear, so start with a short list:

  1. Collect your last city tax and sewer rent bills and the county bill.
  2. Call the city for any sidewalk, demolition or other local charge on the parcel.
  3. Check whether an exemption or STAR registration is active and plan to close it.
  4. Ask both offices for written payoff amounts that are good through your expected closing date.

Doing this before you accept an offer means the figure you negotiate matches what escrow actually pays.

When is the Buffalo grievance period?

Ask the Department of Assessment and Taxation for this year's dates. You file form RP-524 with the department in City Hall Room 101, and a board of city residents reviews it.

When are Buffalo city property taxes due?

Ask the Department of Assessment and Taxation for the current due dates. Erie County bills its part separately and sets its own dates.

Who do I call about my Buffalo assessment?

The Department of Assessment and Taxation at 716-851-5733, option 1 for the Assessor. The office is open 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. in City Hall at 65 Niagara Square.

Where do I pay the Erie County part of a Buffalo tax bill?

Through Erie County Real Property Tax Services, online or at 95 Franklin Street, Room 100. The tax line is 716-858-8333, and the office can give payoff amounts and payment options.

Can I get a payment plan in Buffalo if I am behind?

The Tax Office helps owners obtain court-ordered payment plans, and it notifies owners facing foreclosure for non-payment. Call 716-851-5733 as soon as you know you cannot pay.

Who mails the bill and who sets the value

East Hampton's Receiver of Taxes prepares and mails the bills, and the town Assessor's Office decides the assessed values they rest on. The receiver's office handles over 24,000 bills a year, and each one funds Suffolk County, the town's general fund and a stack of special districts: fire, school, library, lighting, road improvement, water connection and others.

Each parcel falls into its own mix of districts, which is why neighbors can see different totals. The town stretches from Montauk to Wainscott and includes the village of East Hampton and part of Sag Harbor. The Assessor produces the yearly roll, holds ownership and exemption files, and keeps district maps that follow the Suffolk County tax maps. Anyone can view and print a bill from the town's Tax Receiver page, even once collection has closed.

Payment dates and what changes after May 31

At town hall the season opens December 1 and closes May 31. Bills can be paid in two halves and are mailed by mid-December. Pay the first half by January 10 to avoid interest; after that 1% accrues monthly. The second half costs nothing extra until May ends.

On June 1 collection ends. The online and phone systems close, and payments move to the Suffolk County Comptroller, 330 Center Drive, Riverhead, NY 11901, telephone 631-852-3000. Put your tax map number and contact details on the payment, and send it certified if you mail it, so you have proof.

  • The Comptroller takes partial payments of $200 or more, and charges penalty and interest only on the remaining balance.
  • The postmark date counts for mail, but a metered postmark does not.

An undelivered bill does not excuse the owner. Penalties and interest still apply, so request a duplicate from the receiver the moment you realize yours has not come.

STAR and school tax

Owners who have received the older exemption on the bill since 2015, on the same primary residence, keep it, but new homeowners cannot get it. New Basic and Enhanced STAR applicants register with the New York State Department of Taxation and Finance.

For 2026-2027 the income ceiling is $500,000 for Basic. Enhanced STAR, meant for owners aged 65 and over, needs income of $110,750 or less. The credit covers school district taxes only. Selling when tax is still open

Third, is any exemption or STAR benefit tied to your name, and will the buyer need to apply on their own?

Fourth, is the bill going to the right address? A stale mailing address is one way an owner ends up never seeing a bill, and the penalties still apply. Finally, decide how you want to receive the payoff figure. Getting it by email from the receiver or Comptroller gives you a record to hand to the title agent.

If you are selling because the taxes have become a burden, say so early. A cash buyer can take that into account in the offer and can close in a time frame that stops further penalties from adding up.

Closing timeline for a cash sale

A cash buyer removes lender underwriting, so the calendar depends on title work and tax payoffs. In East Hampton the practical question is which office holds the account. Before June 1 the receiver does. After that the Comptroller does, and a figure from the wrong office will not match the payoff.

Start by finding out where your account stands. If everything is current, the closing statement will show only the usual proration. If anything is open, you will need a payoff with penalty and interest, and the title agent will pay it from proceeds. Either way, written figures from the right office and a mailing address that is correct on file help the sale close without delay.

When is the first half of East Hampton property tax due?

The first half is interest-free through January 10. From January 11 the unpaid half grows by 1% a month. The second half stays interest-free until the end of May.

Where do I pay East Hampton tax after May 31?

Send it to the Suffolk County Comptroller, whose office is on Center Drive in Riverhead (631-852-3000). Town online and phone payment shuts down at that point, so mail with your tax map number written on it, certified if you can.

Will the town waive the penalty if I never received my bill?

No. Responsibility rests with the owner whether or not the bill arrived, and penalties and interest keep running. Request a duplicate from the receiver right away.

When must an East Hampton grievance be filed?

The deadline is Grievance Day, falling on May 18 in 2027. Filing starts May 1, when the tentative roll opens. Paper only; email and fax are refused.

Can I sell my East Hampton house while the county holds a tax lien on it?

Yes, provided the lien is cleared at or before closing. The redemption window is twelve months after the lien sale, stretching to thirty-six for a one to three family home. Ask the Comptroller for the payoff and give it to your closing agent.

The Tax Department calls it the largest municipal collection agency in Westchester and says it brings in over a quarter billion dollars a year. The department's phone is 914-989-1550.

The office is open Monday through Friday, 9 am to 5 pm. Checks go to Greenburgh Receiver Of Taxes with the account number written on them. In person the office takes checks and exact-change cash under $10,000, and the lobby has a mailbox where checks, never cash, can be dropped.

Online payment is at the town's municipal tax payments portal. Bank ACH payments carry no fee, and card payments carry a variable rate. Liens cannot be paid online, so anyone with a lien calls or visits the Tax Office.

Due dates and penalties

Greenburgh collects in three windows. Each one ends on a fixed last day, and the office stays open late on that day.

School tax bills are mailed at the end of August, and the next last day after that is January 31. Village taxes are not collected by the town, so residents of a village contact their Village Hall for those due dates.

Two state rules apply. Real Property Tax Law section 922 says a bill that was never mailed or never received does not affect the validity of the tax or interest. Section 920 says the Tax Receiver has no authority to waive penalties for any reason.

How to contest a Greenburgh assessment

Greenburgh runs two tracks: a short informal online review in spring and a formal grievance in June. The assessment should reflect market value as of July 1 of the previous year. Property record cards and a sales map are on the town's Axis GIS site, which is where owners gather comparable sales.

For the informal review, you fill in a portal form with proof of overassessment, and a town appraiser answers within 72 hours. If you agree to a reduction you sign a stipulation and the matter ends for the year. Owners who already met with assessment staff about that year's value must go straight to the formal grievance. Watch the town's assessment calendar for the spring dates, since the window is only about four weeks.

The formal grievance uses form RP-524 and runs from June 1 until 9 pm on the third Tuesday in June. Postmarked-only filings are treated as late. You do not need an attorney. After the final roll on September 15, the Board of Assessment Review mails its results, and an owner has until October 15 to file a small claims assessment review with Westchester County. A reduction first shows up on the Town and County tax bill the following April. The Assessment Department's number is 914-989-1520.

Greenburgh is a town in western Westchester County with 36.1 square miles and six incorporated villages. About half the population lives in the villages, and the rest live in the unincorporated area. Owners occupy 74.0% of homes, the typical owner-occupied home is valued at $697,100, typical monthly rent is $2,316, and median household income is $152,256.

Because the town has ten school districts, two houses a few blocks apart can carry very different school bills, and a house inside a village can carry a village bill on top of the town one.

Which STAR benefit applies to a Greenburgh school tax bill?

The state offers Basic STAR to owner-occupied primary residences and Enhanced STAR to owners aged 65 and over, and both affect only school district tax. Basic STAR is based on the first $30,000 of a home's full value, with an income limit of $500,000 for the credit. Enhanced STAR requires household income of $110,750 or less for the 2026-2027 school year.

The dollar savings depend on which of the ten districts serves the parcel. The Tax Department publishes a 2026-2027 STAR school tax savings sheet and a projected tax sheet for an average household. Registration for the credit goes through the state's Tax Department, not the town. A buyer who plans to live in the house will need to register in their own name, so tell them early.

Handling a tax payoff before selling in Greenburgh

Start with the Tax Office. New owners and anyone who recently paid off a mortgage should call 914-989-1550. Anyone who receives a bill for a property they no longer own should say so. Homeowners with escrowed taxes get a copy of the bill from the Receiver twice a year, so a lender may have paid the current installments already.

  1. Ask the Tax Office which installments are open and whether any lien exists on the account.
  2. Request the figure for any lien directly, since liens are handled in person or by phone and not on the online portal.
  3. Give the payoff numbers to the closing attorney.
  4. Confirm with the buyer's side which village, if any, bills separately.

Town and County tax is billed on a calendar that closes April 30, school tax closes September 30 and January 31, and village tax runs on its own schedule. A closing between those dates needs the current status in writing from each office that bills the parcel. A buyer paying cash can settle the open balance from proceeds at the table, so no penalty keeps building while a lender reviews the file.

When you call, have the account number from your bill, the property address and the closing date ready. If a lender escrows your taxes, ask the lender which installments it has already sent, because the Receiver's records and the lender's records should match before the closing statement is drawn up. Ask for anything you learn to be put in writing, and keep a copy for the closing attorney.

April 30, September 30 and January 31. The office stays open until 7 pm on those dates. Village taxes follow separate dates set by each Village Hall.

No. Real Property Tax Law section 920 gives the Receiver no authority to waive penalties on real estate taxes. Section 922 adds that a bill that was not mailed or not received does not change the tax or interest.

No. Liens cannot be paid online. Call the Tax Office at 914-989-1550 or visit 177 Hillside Avenue to get the amount and pay it.

The third Tuesday in June. Applications on form RP-524 are accepted from June 1 until 9 pm that day. A late or postmark-only application is not reviewed.

  • The EZ-Pay Drive-Thru window behind the Receiver's office, plus satellite offices at Levittown Hall and Rock Hall Museum and a mobile tax office. These give a temporary receipt, and the final one is mailed within seven business days.
  • Online or by phone with a card or electronic check through the Receiver's Payment Center.
  • Mail, with the number 1 stub for a first half, the number 2 stub for a second half, or both stubs for the full year.

Card payments carry a 2.3% convenience fee with a $1.50 minimum. Visa debit is a flat $3.95, and an e-check costs $0.90. The fees go to the payment processor, eGov Strategies, and not to the town. A mailed payment only counts if it has an official U.S. Postal Service cancellation date on or before the last penalty-free day, because a metered postmark is not accepted. Owners aged 65 or older, or with a disability, who own a one to three family home can name a third party to receive a duplicate bill.

Who sets a Hempstead assessment, and when can I challenge it?

Nassau County sets your assessment, and the town does not. The county's Assessment Review Commission is an agency separate from the Department of Assessment, and it takes appeals online through a system called AROW. The commission sits at 240 Old Country Road, 5th Floor, Mineola, and answers at 516-571-3214.

The next tentative roll is dated January 4, 2027, with grievances due March 1, 2027. The final roll follows on April 3, 2028, and court petitions are due May 1, 2028. That roll feeds the 2028/29 school year and the 2029 town and county bills. Filing a grievance costs nothing and needs no lawyer.

If the commission denies your complaint, a Small Claims Assessment Review is open to owners who live in a one, two or three family home. The state charges a $30 filing fee and gives you a 30 day window after the final roll is filed.

Exemptions that can lower a Hempstead bill

The town lists six programs: senior citizens, military service, disability or limited income, STAR, home improvement, and volunteer firefighters and ambulance personnel. Applications go to the Nassau County Department of Assessment, which accepts them year-round, and the filing deadline is January 2. Call 516-571-1500 for forms.

STAR works differently for new applicants. They register with the New York State Department of Taxation and Finance and receive a credit check, not a bill reduction. The Receiver also runs tax forums around the town on exemptions, challenges and early-payment discounts, and sellers who have never claimed anything may find a missed program worth checking before listing.

What happens to Hempstead property tax when I sell?

Unpaid tax stays attached to the parcel until someone pays it, so the sale needs a payoff figure. Settle these items before the closing date:

  • Ask the Receiver at 516-538-1500 which halves of the School and General bills are paid.
  • If a bill shows "arrears," call the Nassau County Treasurer at 516-571-2090 for the amount, since the Receiver no longer holds that tax.
  • Expect exemptions to drop off at transfer. The Department of Assessment removes any exemption a new owner does not qualify for, which is why a buyer's bill can differ a lot from yours.
  • Have the new owner send the ownership and mortgage change form to the Receiver. The town warns owners not to assume an attorney or lender will do it.

A cash purchase can build the tax payoff into the closing statement, so the money never has to come out of your pocket first. If you are behind on Hempstead tax and a lender or lien is involved, get a written payoff from each office first. If you are partway through a bill, a sale in the middle of a penalty period is worth timing, since each month of delay adds another point to the penalty.

The Hempstead housing picture

Hempstead village is dense and mostly renter-heavy, with 17,108 households at 3.37 people each. Owners occupy 47.5% of homes, the middle owner-occupied home is valued at $459,500, rent runs $1,622 at the median, and household income sits at $90,420. The village covers 3.69 square miles and had an estimated 59,819 residents in July 2025. The wider town is the most populous in New York State, at 793,409 people in the 2020 census.

Houses here sell on their own tax bill and condition, so a fresh payoff letter helps more than a neighborhood average.

Frequently asked questions

Where do I pay Hempstead property tax in person?

At the Receiver of Taxes, 200 N Franklin Street, First Floor, Hempstead, NY 11550. The drive-thru window behind the building and the satellite offices at Levittown Hall and Rock Hall Museum also take payments.

Can I still pay school tax to the Hempstead Receiver after May 31?

No. School tax can be paid to the Receiver through May 31, and general tax through August 31. After that, payment goes to the Nassau County Treasurer at 1 West Street in Mineola, 516-571-2090.

Does the Town of Hempstead set my assessment?

No. Nassau County sets assessments, and appeals go to the county's Assessment Review Commission. The next tentative roll is dated January 4, 2027, and grievances are due March 1, 2027.

Will my exemptions pass to the buyer of my Hempstead house?

No. When title transfers, the Nassau County Department of Assessment removes exemptions the new owner is not entitled to. The buyer's first bill can be much higher than yours.

What does it mean if my Hempstead bill says arrears?

It means unpaid tax is already accruing penalties at the Nassau County Treasurer's office. Contact the Treasurer at 516-571-2090 before you pay anything, because the county uses a different penalty schedule than the town.

Which Huntington office bills my property tax?

Two town offices split the job. The Assessor sets values on the 72,500-plus parcels in Huntington and its villages. The Receiver of Taxes prints the bills and collects payment. The Town Board appoints the Assessor, and voters elect the Receiver.

You will find the Receiver at Huntington Town Hall, 100 Main Street, Huntington, NY 11743, phone 631-351-3217. When Huntington property taxes are due

You get one bill, mailed in the second week of December. For 2026/27 the first half is due January 10, 2027, and the second half is due May 31, 2027. January 10, 2027 lands on a Sunday, and a weekend due date rolls to the next business day. Town Hall also posts extended payment hours until 7 pm on June 1, 2027.

Some owners get a few extra days on the second half. Basic STAR recipients have until June 4, 2027, and so do seniors on the Senior Low-Income exemption or Enhanced STAR. After June 1, those seniors can pay only by mail or at the counter.

Mail has become riskier. A federal postmark change effective December 24, 2025 means a letter dropped in a mailbox may carry a later date than the day you sent it.   • If the Board of Assessment Review turns you down, you can take the dispute to court. New York State lists a $30 fee for Small Claims Assessment Review, and the window is 30 days from the final roll.

Suffolk boards sit earlier than boards in most of the state, which use the fourth Tuesday. If you count on the later date, you will miss the Huntington deadline.

If the 2026/27 bill is still open when you list, two dates control your plan. Up to May 31, 2027 the Receiver takes payment.   2. Ask whether a Dix Hills Water District balance sits next to the tax bill.
  3. If the debt has moved to the comptroller, request that office's figure through your expected closing date.
  4. Give both figures to your closing attorney.

Huntington lies on the North Shore of Long Island, with Long Island Sound to its north and Nassau County to its west. Four villages sit inside the town: Asharoken, Huntington Bay, Lloyd Harbor and Northport. Hamlets include Dix Hills, Melville, Commack, Greenlawn and Huntington Station.

The town counts 205,891 residents as of July 2025, in 71,542 households. About 88.7% of homes are owner-occupied, with a median value of $715,600. Median household income is $168,029 and median rent is $2,358. Homes carry high values, which makes each month of 1% interest cost real money.

When is the second half of Huntington property tax due in 2027?

May 31, 2027, with extended hours on June 1, 2027. Owners on Basic STAR, the Senior Low-Income exemption or Enhanced STAR have until June 4, 2027.

Where do I pay late Huntington property tax after May 31?

Send it to the Suffolk County Comptroller at 330 Center Drive, Riverhead, NY 11901. Their number is (631) 852-3000, and the bill adds a 5% penalty plus monthly interest.

What is Grievance Day in Huntington?

The third Tuesday of May, which is May 18 in 2027. The Assessor's Office needs your originally signed complaint on or before that day. Faxed and emailed copies are rejected.

How do I apply for a senior exemption in Huntington?

Call the Assessor's Office at (631) 351-3226 to join the mailing list, then file with proof of income by March 1. The income limit is $58,400.

How Islip property tax collection works

Islip bills through its Receiver of Taxes, and the cycle runs from December to May. Collection opens December 1, bills go out around the second week of December, and the full year's tax is due on or before January 10. Owners who prefer to split the payment pay half by January 10 and the other half by May 31.

You get one bill a year. If your lender escrows the tax, the December bill goes to the lender, and you will receive a statement in February after the first half is paid and another in July after the second. A bill that never reaches you is not a defense, since state law keeps the owner responsible, and the town cannot waive a penalty.

The 2026-2027 tax year begins on December 1, 2026, and details are posted in early to mid December 2026. Taxes become a lien each December 1. Nobody can pay ahead of time, because the Receiver does not know the amount until the warrant arrives from the Suffolk County Legislature.

For a seller, the practical timeline looks like this. In early December the amount becomes known and the lien attaches. By January 10 you either pay everything or the first half. Between January and May each month adds a point to whatever is open. On May 31 the town's window closes. If you plan to list in winter or spring, find out in December which of those stages your bill is in, because the answer decides how much the buyer's title company will hold back at closing.

After January 10 the penalty goes up by one point at the start of each month and stops at 5% for payments made from May 11 to May 31. A partial payment is accepted in person or by mail at any point until May 31, with a minimum of $200 plus any penalty due.

Every application or renewal is due at the Assessor's Office by March 1.

The senior citizen and disability exemptions use a sliding scale for incomes up to $58,400. The Town Board raised that ceiling in October 2022 from the earlier $37,400. Basic STAR covers owner-occupied primary homes where the owners and spouses earn less than $250,000, and it removes the first $30,000 of full value from school tax. Enhanced STAR serves owners aged 65 and up with income under $113,550 for 2027/28, and the state will upgrade Basic to Enhanced automatically. For STAR help call the state at 518-457-2036.

Because tax is a lien from December 1, a sale between December and May needs a payoff for the current year. Ask the Receiver where the bill stands, and then check the title company's search for earlier years.

A cash buyer can take a house with an open tax balance and pay it from the closing proceeds, so penalties stop stacking while the sale is pending. If the house has a senior or disability exemption, tell the buyer early so the restoration amount is not a surprise. Taxes here are billed once a year with a hard lien date, so buyers and title companies look at the status of the current bill first. To the Suffolk County Comptroller, 330 Center Drive, Riverhead, NY 11901. The phone number is (631) 852-3000, and penalty and interest are added.

  • April 1: the final assessment roll. A changed assessment shows up in the billing cycle that begins September 1.

The city has not run a citywide reassessment since 1956, so values on the roll rarely track the sale prices you see around town. Renovations are the exception. Work finished in a given year is reviewed as of that year's December 1, and any new figure appears on the next February roll. If you plan a kitchen or an addition before listing, you can ask the City Appraiser for an estimate of the effect on your assessment.

How do I file a grievance on my New Rochelle assessment?

File Form RP-524 with the Assessor's Office between February 1 and the third Tuesday in February. Applications outside that window cannot be accepted, as the city's grievance page spells out.

  • Look at your tentative roll entry on or after February 1. It shows the assessed value and the assessor's estimate of market value.
  • Gather at least three recent arm's length sales of similar homes close by, matched on size, style, age, condition and lot.
  • Submit the original application in person or by mail. Email and fax copies are refused.
  • File one application for each parcel if you own more than one or your property spans several lots.
  • Ask the Assessor's Office for a hearing time with the Board of Assessment Review after the form is in.

The board is made up of residents appointed by the City Council, and no assessor staff sit on it. If your assessment is fair but the bill still feels heavy, the assessor cannot help, since tax rates are set by the council, the school district and the county legislature. After the grievance stage, most homeowners can go on to Small Claims Assessment Review, but New York requires the local grievance first.

STAR and other exemptions

A new owner who applies for STAR receives it as a check or direct deposit from the state. You register with New York State at tax.ny.gov/star, and the credit requires a primary residence and combined income of all owners and spouses of $500,000 or less.

The older Basic STAR exemption stays in place for people who applied before May 1, 2015, with a combined income under $250,000, and its savings have been capped since 2019. Enhanced STAR is for owners 65 or older within the state income limit, and the state now moves eligible owners over without a new application. Other exemptions are filed with the New Rochelle assessor by December 1.

When you sell, close your STAR registration. Your buyer registers as the new owner of the home.

Selling with unpaid taxes

Open balances get settled as part of the sale, so start by asking the Tax Department for a statement of every unpaid bill on the parcel. Check the city's fee lists as well. Unpaid false alarm charges move onto the next city tax bill after September 30, and restored to roll, sidewalk repair and property maintenance charges move over after December 1.

The deed itself is recorded with the Westchester County Clerk, not at City Hall. The assessor can't change ownership records at the city level and points owners to an attorney, who files the papers with the county clerk.

If you are behind on taxes, tell your closing attorney or title company early so the payoff figures are ready before the closing date. A buyer paying cash still needs those figures, and having them in hand before you sign a contract keeps the closing date from slipping. Bring the latest bills for all four taxing bodies, any fee notices, and the deed information to your first meeting with the attorney.

Frequently asked questions

Which office handles New Rochelle assessment questions?

The Assessor's Office at 515 North Avenue, reachable at (914) 654-2052 on weekdays. It answers questions about assessed value, exemptions and grievance forms but has no say over the tax rate.

When is Grievance Day in New Rochelle?

It falls on the third Tuesday in February. Applications can be filed from February 1 through that Tuesday, and the tentative roll comes out on February 1.

Can I pay a New Rochelle tax bill with a credit card?

Yes, through the city's online payment portal, which also takes e-checks. Convenience fees apply. You can also pay at the City Hall Tax Office, by mail or by direct debit.

Is the New Rochelle school tax due once a year?

No. It is split into two halves, due on or before September 30 and March 31. The library bill rides along with the school bill.

Who pays the March school installment if I sell in the winter?

That depends on your contract and the closing adjustments. The March bill covers January through June, so ask your attorney how the closing statement will divide it.

2026 tax rates by class

New York City sets one rate for each of four tax classes, and the 2026 rates run from 10.848 percent to 19.843 percent of taxable value. A typical house, with one to three dwelling units, falls in Class 1, which carries the highest rate of the four.

Tax year 2026 rates by class

Class 2Larger residential buildings, co-ops and condos12.439%
Class 3Mostly utility property11.108%
Class 4Mostly commercial property10.848%

The Department of Finance rate page carries the full table.

Who assesses and bills property tax in New York City?

The Department of Finance does both jobs. It values every parcel each year, mails the bills and collects the payments, while an independent body called the Tax Commission hears appeals. All five boroughs (Manhattan, Brooklyn, Queens, the Bronx and Staten Island) run under one tax system with no separate county or town collectors.

Property tax made up 41 percent of all city tax dollars collected in the fiscal year that ended June 30, 2026. The city has about 8,584,629 residents and 3,334,088 households, and only 32.8 percent of homes are owner-occupied. Owned homes carry a median value of $777,600.

  • You receive a bill if you pay the tax yourself and have a balance. If a bank or mortgage company pays through escrow, the bill goes to them.
  • Bills are usually mailed and posted online about a month before they are due.
  • Owners remain responsible for paying on time even when no bill arrives, so keep your mailing address current with the department.
  • Water and sewer charges come from the Department of Environmental Protection and are billed apart from the tax.

When are New York City property taxes due?

The city's fiscal year opens each July 1 and closes the next June 30, and how often you pay depends on assessed value. A property assessed at $250,000 or less is billed four times a year, and one assessed above $250,000 is billed twice. The Department of Finance keeps a due dates page with the current calendar.

  • Quarterly payers: the first of July, October, January and April, each with an interest-free grace period through the 15th of the month.
  • Semi-annual payers: July 1 and January 1.
  • Weekends and holidays: a due date on one rolls to the following business day.
  • Mailed payments: the postmark date counts.

Paying ahead earns a discount. Settling the whole year's tax by the July due date or grace date takes 0.50 percent off. Paying the remaining three quarters by October 15 earns 0.33 percent, and paying the final six months by January 15 earns 0.17 percent. Late payment interest is required by law and compounds daily.

How a New York City assessment is worked out

The Department of Finance starts with market value, converts it to an assessed value that is a percentage of that figure, subtracts any exemptions to reach taxable value, multiplies by the class rate, and then subtracts abatements. The result is your yearly bill.

The Notice of Property Value arrives in January each year. It is not a bill and requires no payment. State law limits how far some assessments can move in a single year, so an assessment can take several years to catch up with the market. The department's own example for a one to three family home shows a market value that jumps from $100,000 to $150,000 while the assessed value moves only from 6,000 to 6,360.

A sale settles market value, but the assessment is a separate number. Buyers look at what the next bill will be, so know your current class, exemptions and any abatement before you list.

How do I challenge a New York City assessment?

File an application for correction with the Tax Commission. The deadline is March 15 for Class 1 properties and March 1 for Classes 2, 3 and 4, and late appeals will not be granted.

  • Read the Notice of Property Value first. If it shows an "effective market value," you must show your market value is lower than that figure to win.
  • A Request for Review sent to the Department of Finance is a different step. It covers description errors and is due March 15 for Class 1 and April 1 for other classes.
  • A Request for Review does not replace a timely Tax Commission filing.
  • A Request to Update corrects stale facts such as unit counts or vacant land descriptions.

The Commission can lower an assessment, change a tax class and adjust exemptions. If you plan to list in spring, mark both March dates now, because the outcome sets the tax a buyer inherits.

Lien sales for unpaid tax

A lien sale is possible once the debt passes the minimum for your property type. It transfers the debt to an authorized buyer, not the house itself, but the new lienholder can start a foreclosure if the balance stays unpaid. The city's lien sales page has the schedule and eligibility chart.

For an owner-occupied one-family home, the property tax debt must be at least $5,000 and three years overdue. Two and three family homes follow that rule and can also be listed for $3,000 or more in water and sewer charges outstanding for a year. A one-family owner who owes only water and sewer charges cannot have a lien sold.

  • Homes with a Senior Citizen Homeowners' or Disabled Homeowners' exemption are excluded, as are properties of combat and disabled military service members and those with the State Circuit Breaker. STAR does not protect a property.
  • After a sale, the lienholder may add a 5 percent surcharge, interest of 6, 9 or 16 percent by assessed value, and about $300 in notice costs.
  • Foreclosure can begin within a year of the sale, or sooner if a semi-annual interest payment is more than 30 days late.
  • A waiver of the 5 percent surcharge exists for a primary residence owner with no other city property and combined income of $110,750 or less.

Payment plans if you owe

The Department of Finance offers a standard plan, a deferral program for eligible homeowners called PT AID, and a reduced interest plan for some Class 1 owners. The standard plan allows monthly or quarterly payments for up to 10 years, with no required down payment, although paying something up front lowers each installment.

Interest is set by law and depends on assessed value. For the year that ended June 30, 2026, the rates were 6 percent at $250,000 or less, 9 percent up to $450,000 and 16 percent above that, with 2.5 percent for the reduced interest plan. Ask the department for the rate now in force. A plan cannot be opened once a lien sale or an in rem action has already taken place on the property.

Transfer taxes when you sell

Tax at closing is more than the property tax bill. New York State charges a transfer tax of $2 for each $500 of price, paid by the seller, and every New York City conveyance is reported on Form TP-584-NYC. The state Tax Department has the forms. The buyer pays the 1 percent mansion tax when a residence sells for $1 million or more.

Homes at the upper end carry added city taxes. A residential sale of $3 million or more triggers an extra base tax of $1.25 per $500 paid by the seller, and a supplemental buyer tax of 0.25 to 2.9 percent applies from $2 million. A separate surcharge on high value second homes took effect May 28, 2026, and the department has published a supplemental roll of parcels that might be affected. Ask your closing attorney to request a current statement of what you owe before the closing date.

Frequently asked questions

What is the Class 1 tax rate in New York City?

It is 19.843 percent for tax year 2026. That rate is applied to taxable value, which is a fraction of market value after exemptions.

Is the Notice of Property Value a tax bill?

No. It arrives each January and shows how the Department of Finance valued the property. No payment is due with it.

By when must a Class 1 appeal be filed?

March 15, to the Tax Commission. For Classes 2, 3 and 4 the date is March 1.

Does paying early save money in New York City?

Yes. The full year paid by the July due date or grace date earns 0.50 percent. Paying the rest of the year in October earns 0.33 percent, and in January 0.17 percent.

Will a lien sale take my house?

The sale transfers the debt, not the property. If the new lienholder is not paid or no agreement is reached, a foreclosure case can follow, usually a year after the sale.

Who bills property tax in the Town of North Hempstead?

The Town's Receiver of Taxes bills and collects school and general tax, and the Nassau County Department of Assessment sets the assessments behind the bills. The Receiver's office is at 200 Plandome Road in Manhasset, open Monday to Friday from 9:00 a.m. to 4:45 p.m.

The town sits in Nassau County and has about 238,982 residents (July 1, 2025 estimate). About 79.5% of homes are lived in by their owners, and the median owner-occupied value is $888,000.

Due dates and penalty-free deadlines

School tax and general tax run on separate calendars. The school year is July 1 to June 30, and the general tax year follows the calendar year. If the 10th lands on a weekend or holiday, the penalty-free deadline moves to the next business day.

If the first school half is still open, the unpaid amount is moving toward the county's delinquent roll. Call the Receiver's office for a current figure.

How do you pay a North Hempstead tax bill?

Payment works online, by phone, by mail or at the office. The town's payment vendor handles electronic checks, major credit cards, and Visa or Mastercard debit cards.

  • Electronic check costs a $1.75 flat fee, a credit card costs 2.3% of the amount, and a Visa or Mastercard debit card costs a $3.95 flat fee. State law requires the payer to bear card fees.
  • By mail, send the check to the Manhasset post office box shown on your bill. The postmark must be no later than the due date.
  • Inside the office, a kiosk takes card payments, and a dropbox outside business hours accepts checks and money orders.

Since December 24, 2025, a USPS postmark reflects the date a regional facility processed the mail, so a letter mailed close to a deadline can pick up a later postmark. Mail early. Real Property Law section 925 does not allow a late penalty to be waived, and taxes count as paid only after the payment clears the bank.

School districts and villages

The district that serves your address collects your school tax. If you live inside a village, that village adds a bill of its own. The town's closing guide lists these district codes: Westbury, East Williston, Roslyn, Port Washington, New Hyde Park, Manhasset, Great Neck, Herricks, Mineola, Carle Place, Floral Park, Glenwood Landing and Jericho.

More than two dozen incorporated villages sit inside the town, among them Great Neck Plaza, Kings Point, Lake Success, Manorhaven, Munsey Park, Plandome, Roslyn Harbor, Russell Gardens, Saddle Rock, Sands Point, Thomaston and Williston Park. Villages collect for themselves and may work from assessed values that differ from the county roll. Anyone selling inside a village should also ask the village clerk what is owed and when it is due. A dispute over which district a house belongs to goes to that district or the state education commissioner, because the town has no say.

How the school and general tax split affects a sale

Each half-year bill covers a different slice of time, so the seller and buyer settle up based on which months each bill paid for. The first-half school levy covers July 1 to December 31, the second-half school levy covers January 1 to June 30, the first-half general levy covers January 1 to June 30, and the second-half general levy covers July 1 to December 31.

The Receiver's closing guide says to line the closing date up against these periods. Say you close in November: that date sits in the first school half and the second general half. An April closing sits in the second school half and the first general half. Get a written payoff from your attorney or title company before closing. If a deadline is close, ask the town for the exact penalty.

Exemptions and restored taxes after a sale

An exemption usually stays with the seller, not the deed. Your buyer applies separately through the Nassau County Department of Assessment. If an exemption ends because of a sale, Nassau County may add prorated restored taxes of up to one year to a later bill, and because of the county assessment calendar this can take up to two years to show up.

New owners must tell the Receiver of Taxes, and the incorporated village if there is one, about the new ownership, mailing address and mortgage escrow, which keeps bills from going to the wrong place. Improvements, including work done before a sale that was never reported, can raise the assessed value beyond the 6% cap.

The county administers these programs:

  • STAR cuts school tax only. Basic STAR is open to any age with income of $500,000 or less, and Enhanced STAR is for owners 65 and older.
  • A senior citizens exemption reducing county, town and school tax by 5% to 65% on a sliding income scale, with the top 65% tier at $47,000 of income or less.
  • Disability, military service, and volunteer firefighter and ambulance exemptions.
  • A home improvement exemption that decreases over eight years on qualifying work.

The statewide STAR rules are covered in our New York STAR guide.

How do you challenge a North Hempstead assessment?

File an application for correction with the Nassau County Assessment Review Commission, which is separate from the Department of Assessment. The next window follows the tentative roll set January 4, 2027, with filing open through March 1, 2027.

Filing is online through AROW, in person at 240 Old Country Road in Mineola, or on a paper form you request. It costs nothing, and you can handle it yourself or use a representative. The Commission asks for sales of comparable homes, and its online sales locator helps you find them. A denial leaves one more option, a Small Claims Assessment Review petition in court. The Receiver of Taxes does not set assessments and cannot change them, and a village that keeps its own roll requires a separate filing with the Village Assessor.

If North Hempstead property tax goes unpaid

Once a bill goes unpaid, it passes to the Nassau County Treasurer. For the towns of Hempstead, North Hempstead and Oyster Bay, the Treasurer's Tax Records department handles both delinquent general and school tax, starting June 1 for school tax and September 1 for general tax.

The county's page for delinquent taxes shows which payment methods are open in each period. Personal checks are accepted for part of the year, credit card and electronic check payments run later, and the final day to pay before the lien sale falls at 3:00 PM on a Wednesday in February. Once a lien exists, you cannot pay it online. It takes a bank cashier's check or cash.

The state's lien and foreclosure rules are in our tax lien guide. Selling with tax still owed? Get the payoff in writing, and your closing attorney can pay it out of the proceeds. The rate for your parcel is printed on your bill, and the Receiver's office can explain it.

Frequently asked questions

When is North Hempstead general tax due?

First-half general tax is due January 1, 2027, with no penalty through February 10, 2027. The second half comes due July 1, 2027 and is penalty-free through August 10, 2027.

Where do I pay my North Hempstead taxes in person?

Visit 200 Plandome Road in Manhasset on a weekday between 9:00 a.m. and 4:45 p.m. and bring your bill. Cards go through the kiosk, and checks or money orders can go in the dropbox.

What happens if I miss the November 10 school tax deadline?

The first-half school bill becomes late, and delinquent amounts are collected by the Nassau County Treasurer. Contact the Receiver's office about penalties.

Who do I call to appeal my assessment?

Contact the Nassau County Assessment Review Commission, which lists a phone line for forms and questions. The Receiver of Taxes has no power over assessments.

Do I keep my STAR benefit if I sell and move?

Not on the house you sold. Close your registration with the state at the sale, and the buyer registers once they live there as a primary residence.

Who sends the property tax bill for a house in Rochester?

The City of Rochester sends one bill that covers the city and the Rochester City School District, and Monroe County sends a second bill. A house inside the city limits therefore carries two separate tax accounts, and a buyer or title company will ask about both.

City bills go out by mail each July to owners who do not pay through a mortgage escrow. Under New York Real Property Tax Law section 922, the owner still has to pay on time if a bill never arrives. Monroe County bills separately and mails its bill on December 31 for city properties. For county questions, call the Monroe County Real Property Tax Service Office.

Three city offices matter if you are about to sell:

  • Bureau of Assessment, City Hall Room 101A, 30 Church Street: values, exemptions and assessment complaints.
  • Treasury Bureau, City Hall, 30 Church Street: unpaid taxes, payment agreements and the amount owed on a given parcel.
  • Rochester Water Department and the Municipal Code Violations Bureau: water charges and code fines, which the city's online property tool does not show in full.

The four installment due dates

Rochester splits the city and school bill into four installments: July 31, September 30, January 31 and March 31. The 2026 cycle runs July 31 and September 30, 2026, then January 31 and March 31, 2027. If an earlier installment is still open, check whether the balance rolled forward before you list the house.

A late installment collects interest at 1 percent per month. If a deadline lands on a weekend, the following Monday is the cutoff. The city encourages electronic payment. Mailed payments go to the Binghamton post office box named on the bill coupon, with the check made out to the City Treasurer and the installment coupon enclosed. Payments under a tax agreement are the exception: those go straight to the Treasury Bureau at City Hall.

Throw away any old return label from a prior year, since the city's mailing address changed. An owner paying in full by July 31 should send the first installment coupon, because the city built that coupon to handle either a full payment or the first quarter.

A one, two or three family house in Rochester is taxed at the homestead rate, which for 2026-27 combines to $18.2157 per $1,000 of assessed value once city, school, county and the Pure Waters capital charge are added. Everything that is not a one to three family home or some vacant land pays the non-homestead rate.

Water is billed separately unless the account becomes substantially delinquent, at which point it can land on the tax bill. Code enforcement charges can be added to the bill too.

How do I contest a Rochester assessment?

File a complaint with the Rochester Board of Assessment Review by 8 p.m. Eastern on the third Tuesday in March. In 2027 that Tuesday is March 16, and the form has to be received at the Bureau of Assessment, City Hall Room 101A, by that hour.

The assessment calendar runs in this order each year:

  • February 1: exemption applications and renewals are due, and the taxable status date falls here.
  • March 1: the tentative roll is filed with New York State.
  • Third Tuesday in March: complaint deadline. Hearings run through March and April.
  • May 1: the final roll is filed.
  • May 30: Small Claims Assessment Review filing deadline.
  • July 1 through January 1: informal assessment reviews are available.

The informal review window is the quiet option for an owner who missed the March deadline. Bring photos and a recent appraisal or comparable sales if you want the assessor to look at condition problems.

Exemptions for Rochester homeowners

The city lists STAR, a senior citizen exemption, military service exemptions, a disability exemption, a capital improvement exemption and a clergy exemption. Every application has to reach the Bureau of Assessment by February 1, 2027. The Bureau runs an exemption hotline at 585-428-6994.

Income and age thresholds from the city's exemptions page:

  • Enhanced STAR: owner age 65 or older, or turning 65 by December 31, 2027, with household income up to $113,550 in 2025.
  • Senior citizen exemption: owner age 65 or older (or a surviving spouse 62 or older) with income up to $58,400 in the prior year, renewed each year.
  • Disability exemption: same $58,400 income cap, for owners receiving certain disability benefits or certified as legally blind.
  • Capital improvement: one and two family houses with at least $3,000 of qualifying improvements.

New STAR recipients get a check from New York State instead of a bill reduction, so they register with the state tax department. If you have been receiving a senior or disability exemption, know that the city can add a supplemental tax when a prior owner's exemption ends through a transfer or death.

Unpaid taxes and tax liens

Rochester suspended its tax lien sales in 2020 until further notice, but the lien itself still exists. A lien starts when the annual tax is levied, and once the bill has gone unpaid for one year it counts as delinquent.

When the city ran its sales, an owner got a notice and had twenty days to clear the debt, and a buyer of the lien (the city used American Tax Funding Services) collected the debt from then on. Owners could apply for a delinquency agreement with the Director of Finance at least twenty days before a sale date. Liens did not qualify for sale if a payment agreement was in force, if bankruptcy law restricted enforcement, or if a tax certiorari proceeding for the same year was pending. The state redemption rule for delinquent liens is a two-year period under RPTL section 1110, which a taxing district can lengthen for homes.

The Treasury Bureau handles delinquency questions at 585-428-6940. Ask it for a payoff figure in writing before you accept an offer on a house with unpaid years.
